chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah, from Muhammad ibn Abi Yunus, from Yazid ibn Ishaq, from Harun ibn Hamzah al-Ghanawi, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man buys palm trees to cut them for their trunks, but leaves them standing, and the palms bear fruit. He said: 'The fruit is for him, unless the owner of the land watered it and tended to it.'

key_terms.قَامَ عَلَيْهِ: he tended to it / took care of it

ai.seo_question: Who owns the fruit if palm trees are sold for their trunks but left standing?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies the principle of *ikhtilaf al-amlak* (divergence of ownership) in agricultural sales, establishing that the buyer of the trunk retains rights to the fruit unless the seller retains the duty of irrigation and maintenance. This ruling highlights the Shia juristic emphasis on the actual labor and resource contribution of the landowner as the determining factor for fruit ownership, rather than mere title to the tree. It serves as a foundational precedent for modern Islamic commercial law regarding lease-to-own or partial-sale arrangements in agriculture.
